# Overview

This is a running development log for the Fantasee Forge prediction model.

The idea behind Fantasee Forge is fairly simple: take historical NFL data, turn it into useful player-level features, train a model to predict fantasy production, and eventually use those predictions to power the website.

I'm deliberately documenting the process as I build it rather than only recording the final model. There are quite a few decisions involved in getting from raw NFL data to a prediction, and I want to be able to look back and understand **why something was done**, not just what the final code happens to do.

The current modelling pipeline looks roughly like this:

<div style="text-align:center; margin: 2rem 0;">

**NFL data → raw files → DuckDB → staging → features → training data → model → evaluation**

</div>

The website itself comes later. For now, the priority is getting a model that can be tested properly and understanding where its predictions are coming from.

# Setup

The project is being developed on Windows using PowerShell, Python, SQL and DuckDB. Python work is being done inside the project's `.venv` virtual environment.

The project lives at:

`C:\Users\bough\Projects\FantaseeForge`

The initial project structure was set up around separate areas for data, SQL, Python, models and eventually the website. The main database is:

`database/fantasee_forge.duckdb`

I also set up Git/GitHub early because I want the project to be reproducible and to have a proper history of changes rather than ending up with a collection of scripts that only work on my machine.

# Data

The first stage was getting NFL data into the project in a form that could be reused without downloading everything every time.

The initial ingestion work was handled through **`python/ingest/download_data.py`**. This uses `nflreadpy` to obtain the relevant nflverse data and saves the downloaded datasets as Parquet files under the project's raw-data directory.

The important part of this setup is the caching behaviour. Once a dataset has been downloaded, the pipeline checks whether the corresponding local file already exists and reuses it rather than downloading it again.

That matters for two reasons. Firstly, it makes development much quicker. Secondly, it means I can repeatedly rebuild the DuckDB tables without repeatedly hitting the source data.

The initial raw data collection included the player statistics, schedules, rosters and snap-count information needed for the modelling work.

# Database

Once the raw data was available, the next step was getting it into DuckDB.

The database was built as a small analytical warehouse rather than trying to do all the transformation work directly in Python. The intention is to keep the data pipeline reasonably transparent:

**raw data → staging → features → model-ready data**.

This also means I can inspect intermediate tables directly in DuckDB, which has been particularly useful while developing the model.

The main staging tables eventually became:

| Table                  | Purpose                                             |
| ---------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| `staging.player_game`  | Player-level game statistics and PPR fantasy points |
| `staging.snap_usage`   | Offensive and defensive snap counts/share           |
| `staging.team_passing` | Team passing attempts by game                       |

One of the first lessons here was not to assume that the database looked exactly like the original plan.

# Player Data

I checked the structure of `staging.player_game` with DuckDB's `DESCRIBE` command.

The table contains the player-level statistics needed for the first model, including:

* player and game identifiers
* season and week
* team and opponent
* passing statistics
* rushing statistics
* receiving statistics
* `fantasy_points_ppr`

The last column was particularly useful because it meant the PPR scoring had already been calculated upstream.

There was originally an assumption in the pipeline that a separate `staging.player_game_scored` table would exist. A validation script initially referenced that table, but the actual database did not contain it.

Rather than create another unnecessary table just to match the original plan, I changed the pipeline to use the existing `fantasy_points_ppr` column.

The validation script was updated accordingly in **`python/validation/validate_database.py`**.

The important check here was simply that `staging.player_game` existed and contained rows.

That gave us confidence that the rest of the feature-building process was operating on the actual database structure rather than an assumed one.

# Snap Data

Next I checked `staging.snap_usage`.

The purpose of this table is to give the model information about opportunity that isn't obvious from fantasy points alone.

For example, two players might both score 12 fantasy points, but one could have played almost every offensive snap while the other only played half of them.

The table contains:

* offensive snaps
* offensive snap percentage
* defensive snaps
* defensive snap percentage
* player/team/game identifiers

The field that became particularly interesting later was `offense_pct`.

At this point I wasn't assuming snap share would improve the model. I was simply making sure the data existed and understanding what was available.

# Team Passing

I also checked `staging.team_passing`.

This table gives the number of passing attempts made by each team in each game.

The reasoning for keeping this separate was that fantasy production doesn't happen in isolation. A receiver's opportunities, for example, are partly dependent on how much the team throws the ball.

Again, this was treated as a feature to test rather than something that was automatically assumed to improve predictions.

# Validation

Before building the model, I wanted a reasonably clean path from the player-game data into a training dataset.

The first validation script was **`python/validation/validate_database.py`**.

Its purpose was deliberately simple: make sure the tables we were relying on actually existed and weren't empty.

This caught the `player_game_scored` issue early.

That might seem like a minor check, but it is exactly the sort of thing that is worth checking before spending time debugging a model that is actually working from the wrong table.

# Rolling Features

With the staging data understood, I created the first feature table:

**`sql/features/player_rolling.sql`**

This created `features.player_rolling`.

The first features were based mainly on recent player performance:

| Feature                   | What it represents                                 |
| ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| `fantasy_points_avg_l2`   | Average PPR points over the previous 2 games       |
| `fantasy_points_avg_l4`   | Average PPR points over the previous 4 games       |
| `fantasy_points_avg_l8`   | Average PPR points over the previous 8 games       |
| `targets_avg_l4`          | Average targets over the previous 4 games          |
| `receptions_avg_l4`       | Average receptions over the previous 4 games       |
| `receiving_yards_avg_l4`  | Average receiving yards over the previous 4 games  |
| `rushing_attempts_avg_l4` | Average rushing attempts over the previous 4 games |
| `rushing_yards_avg_l4`    | Average rushing yards over the previous 4 games    |

There was one important detail in the SQL.

The rolling windows deliberately stopped at the **previous** row rather than including the current row.

That was done to avoid leakage.

If I'm trying to predict a player's next game, I can use their previous four games. I can't use the result of the game I'm trying to predict.

This was one of the main principles behind the feature engineering from the beginning.

# Target

Once the historical features existed, I needed to define exactly what the model was supposed to predict.

That was done in:

**`sql/features/model_training.sql`**

The target was created using `LEAD()` over each player's games.

In other words, each row contains information available around one game, and `target_fantasy_points` contains the fantasy points from that player's next recorded game.

I chose the next recorded game rather than simply saying "next calendar week".

That means bye weeks don't need any special handling. If a player plays Week 9 and then Week 11, the Week 9 row points to Week 11 as the next target.

# Target Check

I wanted to check this rather than assume the `LEAD()` was correct.

The check was run against Tom Brady and included the player's season, week, current fantasy points, target fantasy points, target season and target week.

The results showed the expected behaviour.

For example, a Week 9 game pointed to Week 11 rather than Week 10, which demonstrated that bye weeks were being handled naturally.

The check also crossed the season boundary correctly, with a player's final game of one season pointing to their first recorded game of the next season where appropriate.

The final game for a player had a `NULL` target, which is also what we want because there is no future game in the dataset.

This check was important because a target-shifting mistake can make an apparently excellent model completely misleading.

# Clean Data

The next script was:

**`sql/features/model_training_clean.sql`**

This removed rows where there wasn't a usable target or where the required historical features weren't available.

The resulting training table contained:

| Check            | Result |
| ---------------- | -----: |
| Rows             | 38,357 |
| Distinct players |  1,197 |
| First season     |   2019 |
| Last season      |   2026 |

The presence of 2026 here isn't a problem. The current season is incomplete, so only a small number of 2026 rows are currently available.

For model evaluation, I would not randomly mix those rows into the historical training/test split.

# Model V1

The first model was deliberately kept fairly simple.

The Python script was:

**`python/models/train.py`**

The model used eight features based on recent player production and opportunity:

* recent fantasy points
* recent targets
* recent receptions
* recent receiving yards
* recent rushing attempts
* recent rushing yards

The model itself was an XGBoost regression model.

I used a time-based split rather than a random split. The training data covered:

**2019–2024**

and the test data was:

**2025**

This is much closer to how the model will eventually be used.

If I randomly split the rows, information from later seasons could end up in the training data while earlier seasons are used for testing. That wouldn't represent the real-world problem very well.

# V1 Results

The first model loaded 38,084 usable historical rows.

The split was:

| Dataset  |   Rows |
| -------- | -----: |
| Training | 32,412 |
| Testing  |  5,672 |

The results on the 2025 test season were:

| Metric               |        V1 |
| -------------------- | --------: |
| MAE                  | **4.628** |
| RMSE                 | **6.313** |
| Spearman correlation | **0.659** |

These numbers became our initial benchmark.

The model was saved as:

**`models/fantasee_forge_xgb.joblib`**

# Baseline

I didn't want to judge the XGBoost model in isolation.

The next script was:

**`python/models/baseline.py`**

The baseline simply used the player's four-game average fantasy points as the prediction.

That gave:

| Metric | Baseline |
| ------ | -------: |
| MAE    |    4.767 |
| RMSE   |    6.681 |

Compared with that, XGBoost produced:

| Metric | Baseline |        V1 |
| ------ | -------: | --------: |
| MAE    |    4.767 | **4.628** |
| RMSE   |    6.681 | **6.313** |

So V1 was doing better than simply saying "this player normally scores around X points".

The improvement wasn't enormous, but it was enough to show that the model was learning something beyond the simple rolling average.

# Positions

I also wanted to avoid hiding everything behind one overall number.

The model was therefore evaluated separately for QB, RB, TE and WR.

The V1 results were:

| Position |  Rows |   MAE |  RMSE |
| -------- | ----: | ----: | ----: |
| QB       |   611 | 6.676 | 8.349 |
| RB       | 1,483 | 4.765 | 6.613 |
| TE       | 1,210 | 3.793 | 5.309 |
| WR       | 2,368 | 4.441 | 5.974 |

This is useful because the positions behave differently and have different scoring distributions.

It also gives us something to monitor as new features are introduced.

# Ranking

The other metric I added was Spearman rank correlation.

The reason is that Fantasee Forge isn't ultimately just trying to tell someone:

> "Player X will score 14.7 points."

The site will also need to rank players.

So I wanted a metric that tells me whether the model's ordering of players broadly lines up with the actual ordering.

V1 produced:

**Spearman = 0.659**

I'm treating this as a complementary metric rather than replacing MAE and RMSE with it.

# V2

At this point the basic model was working, but it was still heavily based on historical player production.

The next question was whether we could give it more information about **opportunity**.

This led to V2.

The two additional features were:

| Feature                     | Reason                      |
| --------------------------- | --------------------------- |
| `offense_pct_avg_l4`        | Recent offensive snap share |
| `team_pass_attempts_avg_l4` | Recent team passing volume  |

The idea was that recent fantasy production tells us what happened, while snap share and team passing volume might tell us something about the opportunity behind that production.

# Opportunity

The opportunity features were created in:

**`sql/features/player_opportunity.sql`**

This joined the player-game data to `staging.snap_usage` and `staging.team_passing`.

The rolling features were again calculated using previous games only.

That means the model isn't allowed to see the current game's snap share or passing volume when trying to predict that game's result.

That distinction is important.

Using a player's *previous* snap share is legitimate.

Using the snap share they actually received in the game we're trying to predict would be leakage.

# Coverage

Before using the opportunity data, I checked how complete the snap-count join was.

The query counted total rows, rows with snap data and rows without it.

The result was:

That means roughly **99.9% of the player-game rows had snap data**.

This was important because a feature can look promising in theory but be fairly useless if most of the historical data is missing.

That wasn't the case here.

# V2 Model

Rather than overwriting V1, I copied the training script and created:

**`python/models/train_v2.py`**

This is important because I want to be able to reproduce and compare different model versions later.

V2 used the original eight features plus:

* `offense_pct_avg_l4`
* `team_pass_attempts_avg_l4`

The resulting model was saved separately as:

**`models/fantasee_forge_xgb_v2.joblib`**

The same time-based evaluation was kept:

**Training: 2019–2024**

**Testing: 2025**

Keeping the test period the same makes the comparison between V1 and V2 much more useful.

# Importance

The next thing I wanted to understand was what the V2 model was actually paying attention to.

The script for this was:

**`python/models/feature_importance_v2.py`**

The resulting feature importance was:

<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Feature</th>
<th>Importance</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td><code>fantasy_points_avg_l8</code></td><td>0.5804</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>fantasy_points_avg_l4</code></td><td>0.1609</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>fantasy_points_avg_l2</code></td><td>0.0636</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>offense_pct_avg_l4</code></td><td>0.0503</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>rushing_attempts_avg_l4</code></td><td>0.0293</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>rushing_yards_avg_l4</code></td><td>0.0270</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>targets_avg_l4</code></td><td>0.0267</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>receiving_yards_avg_l4</code></td><td>0.0234</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>team_pass_attempts_avg_l4</code></td><td>0.0196</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>receptions_avg_l4</code></td><td>0.0189</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>

This is probably the most interesting result so far.

The model is heavily driven by recent fantasy production.

In particular, `fantasy_points_avg_l8` accounts for 0.5804 of the model's built-in feature importance.

The next two fantasy-performance features are also near the top.

Taken together:

`fantasy_points_avg_l8 + fantasy_points_avg_l4 + fantasy_points_avg_l2`

account for approximately **80.5%** of the reported feature importance.

That tells me that, at the moment, Fantasee Forge is primarily learning:

> **"How has this player been performing recently?"**

rather than:

> **"What is the opportunity and matchup around this player?"**

That's actually a useful finding.

It gives us a much clearer idea of what the model currently is.

# Current Picture

At the moment, the model is in a reasonably useful experimental state.

We have a reproducible data path from nflverse into DuckDB, a set of leakage-conscious historical features, a clearly defined next-game target, a time-based train/test split, a simple baseline, position-level evaluation, rank correlation and two versions of the XGBoost model.

The biggest result so far isn't actually that V2 is slightly better than V1.

It's that we now know where the model is getting most of its signal.

Recent player fantasy production dominates the current model, particularly the eight-game average.

The opportunity features are being used, with offensive snap share having noticeably more importance than team passing volume, but adding them has not yet produced a large change in the 2025 test results.

That gives us a much better starting point for the next stage.

# Next

I don't want to just keep adding features and hoping the numbers improve.

The next experiment should be a controlled **ablation test**.

The idea is to compare:

| Model | Features                                   |
| ----- | ------------------------------------------ |
| V1    | Original player-history features           |
| V2    | Player history + snap share + team passing |
| V2a   | Player history + snap share                |
| V2b   | Player history + team passing              |

All four should use the same training period, the same 2025 test period and the same evaluation metrics.

That should tell us whether the new opportunity variables are actually adding useful information, and if so, which one is doing it.

Only after that would I start adding more complicated things such as defensive matchup information.

The aim is to build the model in a way where I can explain **why each feature exists and whether it actually helps**, rather than ending up with a large collection of variables that happen to produce a good-looking number on one test.

# Summary

The project has moved from raw NFL data to a functioning first prediction model.

### Development note

This document should be treated as a **living Quarto document**. As the model develops, the next sections can be added underneath this point rather than rewriting the history each time.

That way the final project will contain a record of how the model went from the initial baseline through opportunity features, matchup features, backtesting and eventually the production model used by the website.
